content: A pterygium is a fleshy, wing-shaped growth that originates from the conjunctiva and extends across the limbus onto the cornea. Its prevalence varies significantly across different regions of the world. Ultraviolet light exposure is considered a major factor in the development of pterygia. This condition can impair vision, restrict eye movements, and cause symptoms such as eye irritation, a sensation of a foreign body in the eye, and dryness. In severe cases, particularly in susceptible individuals, the pterygium may grow to cover the entire corneal surface, obstructing the visual axis. Surgical removal is the only effective treatment for pterygium, but recurrence is a common issue. Simple excision, which involves removing the pterygium and leaving the sclera bare, has a recurrence rate of up to 80%. However, combining pterygium excision with a tissue graft significantly reduces the risk of recurrence. In conjunctival autograft surgery, a piece of conjunctival tissue, along with limbal tissue, is harvested from another part of the patient’s eye and used to cover the area where the pterygium was removed. Another surgical option is the amniotic membrane graft, where a donor amniotic membrane is placed over the limbus and bare sclera after pterygium excision. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of conjunctival autograft surgery (with or without adjunctive therapy) compared to amniotic membrane graft surgery (with or without adjunctive therapy) for the treatment of pterygium. Additionally, the review aimed to assess whether the use of mitomycin C (MMC) improved surgical outcomes and to compare the direct and indirect costs of these procedures. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases, such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, and others, covering literature from as early as 1946 to November 2015. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Randomized controlled trials comparing conjunctival autograft surgery with amniotic membrane graft surgery in patients with primary or recurrent pterygium were included in the review. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, assessed the full-text reports of potentially eligible trials, and extracted data from the included studies. The primary outcome of interest was the risk of pterygium recurrence at three and six months post-surgery. Meta-analyses were conducted using random-effects models, and risk ratios were calculated to compare the two surgical techniques. A total of 20 studies involving 1947 eyes from 1866 participants were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in eight countries, including Brazil, China, Cuba, Egypt, Iran, Thailand, Turkey, and Venezuela. The overall risk of bias was unclear, as many studies did not adequately describe their randomization methods or masking procedures to prevent performance and detection bias. The risk ratio for pterygium recurrence with conjunctival autograft compared to amniotic membrane transplant was 0.87 (95% CI 0.43 to 1.77) at three months and 0.53 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.85) at six months. These results included participants with both primary and recurrent pterygia. Subgroup analysis revealed that for primary pterygia, the risk ratio was 0.92 (95% CI 0.37 to 2.30) at three months and 0.58 (95% CI 0.27 to 1.27) at six months. For recurrent pterygia, the risk ratio at six months was 0.45 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.99). When a study with unclear allocation concealment was excluded in a sensitivity analysis, the risk ratio for recurrence at six months was 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.62) for both primary and recurrent pterygia. One study reported on clinical improvement, defined as the absence of recurrence, and found that 93.8% of participants in the conjunctival limbal autograft group and 93.3% in the amniotic membrane transplant group showed no recurrence at three months post-surgery. Data on other outcomes, such as the need for repeat surgery, vision-related quality of life, and surgical costs, were insufficient for analysis. Adverse events were reported in 13 studies and included complications such as granuloma, pyogenic granuloma, and increased intraocular pressure. None of the studies reported cases of induced astigmatism. In conclusion, conjunctival autograft surgery is associated with a lower risk of pterygium recurrence at six months post-surgery compared to amniotic membrane transplant, particularly in patients with recurrent pterygia. However, there is limited evidence comparing the two techniques in terms of visual acuity outcomes, vision-related quality of life, and surgical costs. Further research is needed to address these gaps and to evaluate the role of adjunctive mitomycin C in reducing recurrence rates.
